contents.reason: The Laplacian identities collected there are the product and chain rules for the Laplacian, whose consumers are the mean value property, the maximum principle and the Poisson kernel; none of those is developed from this page's declared prerequisites, and this page needs the Laplacian only to state the two Green identities.

contents.reason: The expansion a x (b x c) = (c.a)b - (b.a)c is cross-product algebra with no consumer here: every identity on this page is proved by direct coordinate expansion from def-cross-product-in-r3, and none of the three routes that could have used it (the divergence and curl of a cross product, the curl of a curl, the curl as the antisymmetric part of the total derivative) does. Its natural home is the published cross-product material on regular-surfaces-and-surface-integrals, and published pages are not retrofitted, so it has no page to go to.

contents.name: Section 4.1.2 Vector Potentials

Lemma 4.1.13 (a vector potential may be chosen with a specified vanishing component)
contents.reason: CLP-4 reaches Theorem 4.1.16 by constructing a vector potential with third component zero and integrating the remaining two coordinates, and this lemma is the internal step that normalises that component. This page reaches the vector potential by the homotopy formula A(x) = the integral over t in [0,1] of t B(a+t(x-a)) x (x-a), which produces its potential directly and never normalises a component, so the lemma is a step of a route this page does not take rather than a result it declines to prove.

contents.reason: Deriving the heat equation turns the divergence theorem into a statement about a time-dependent temperature field and then studies that partial differential equation; no notion of a partial differential equation, of an initial value problem for one, or of a time-dependent field is available among this page's declared prerequisites.

Equation 4.2.10 and section 4.2.3 (buoyancy and the centre of mass motion law)
contents.reason: Buoyancy identifies the boundary flux of a hydrostatic pressure field with a weight, which is a statement about a physical model rather than about the vector calculus this page develops; the mathematical content is exactly the vector form of the divergence theorem already scaffolded.

contents.name: Equation 4.2.11 and section 4.2.4 (torque and angular momentum)
contents.reason: The torque identity is a rigid body statement whose only mathematical ingredient is the same vector form of the divergence theorem; angular momentum, rigid motion and their time derivatives have no definition among this page's declared prerequisites.

contents.name: Theorem 4.2.12 and section 4.2.5 (solving Poisson's equation)
contents.reason: The solution formula for Poisson's equation rests on the Newtonian potential, on differentiating an improper convolution integral through its singularity, and on Green's second identity applied on a punctured region; the first two of those are the subject matter of the Poisson problem page and not of the integral theorems here.

The four equivalent conditions on a simply connected solid region
contents.reason: Corral states the equivalence of a potential, path independence, zero circulation and a vanishing curl on a simply connected region. Simple connectedness is a homotopy notion, and no homotopy of paths is available among this page's declared prerequisites, so the star-shaped case is what this page proves; the simply connected case belongs with the machinery that computes when a closed field is exact.
